name: Ayeik Ma Htwet Pagoda
significance: A brick stupa in Aungmyethazan Township, Mandalay, which a stone inscription credits to King Kyansittha of the Pagan kingdom in 1064; relics of the Buddha are enshrined in a chamber within it.
story: The pagoda is said to cast no shadow in sunlight, answering Kyansittha's vow that its shadow should never fall again in any of his future births.

name: Mahabodhi Temple, Bagan
significance: A Theravada temple at Bagan raised in the early 13th century under King Htilominlo as a copy of the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya; over 450 Buddha images fill the niches of its tall pyramidal tower, which was repaired after the 1975 Bagan earthquake.

name: Wat Phra That Phanom
style: Lao stupa form with Dvaravati, Khmer and Cham elements
significance: The chief Buddhist stupa of northeastern Thailand, standing near the Mekong in That Phanom district and enshrining what tradition holds to be the Buddha's breast bone; archaeology dates the earliest structure on the site to the 7th or 8th century, and the pagoda has been restored in modern times with royal Thai patronage.
story: The That Phanom Chronicle says the Buddha asked Mahakasyapa to carry his breast-bone relic to Phu Kamphra after his death, and that the disciple with five hundred arhats raised the stupa over it there.

name: Sakya Man Aung Pagoda
significance: A Buddhist temple about a kilometre northeast of the royal palace at Mrauk U, commissioned in 1629 by King Thiri Thudhamma Raza; its stupa is laid out on an eight-petalled lotus plan and turns from an octagonal form to a bell above nine rising tiers.

name: Giác Lâm Pagoda
significance: A Buddhist pagoda in the Tân Bình district of Ho Chi Minh City, founded in 1744 by Lý Thụy Long during the rule of the Nguyễn lord Nguyễn Phúc Khoát. Amitabha dominates its main altar, with Shakyamuni and four bodhisattvas set before him, and a bodhi tree brought from Sri Lanka in 1953 grows in its garden.

name: Hội Khánh Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (with Ksitigarbha and other bodhisattvas)
significance: A Buddhist temple at Thủ Dầu Một in Bình Dương province, built in 1741, destroyed in 1861 during the French colonial conflict and rebuilt soon after by Thích Chánh Đắc. Between 1923 and 1926 anti-colonial activists, among them Ho Chi Minh's father Nguyễn Sinh Sắc, met within its walls.

name: Pu Tuo Si Temple
significance: A Chinese Buddhist temple in Kota Kinabalu, Sabah, completed in 1980. Its Daxiong Baodian main hall holds a large Buddha image flanked by Guanyin on the left and Dashizhi on the right.

name: Maha Wizaya Pagoda
deity: Buddha (enshrined relics given by the King of Nepal)
significance: A stupa in Dagon Township, Yangon, built in 1980 to commemorate the First Congregation for the purification of the Buddha Sasana, out of which came the State Sangha Maha Nayaka Committee. It enshrines relics contributed by the King of Nepal, and Ne Win consecrated its crowning umbrella.

name: Vĩnh Nghiêm Pagoda
significance: A large pagoda in District 3 of Ho Chi Minh City, begun in 1964 by the monks Thích Tâm Giác and Thích Thanh Kiểm and named for an 11th-century predecessor in Bắc Giang province. It was the first in Vietnam to render traditional Vietnamese temple architecture in concrete, and its seven-storey, 40 m tower was built with help from the Japan–Vietnam Friendship Association.

name: Uruwala Valagamba Raja Maha Vihara
significance: An ancient Buddhist temple at Uruwala in the Gampaha District, formally protected by the Sri Lankan government as an archaeological site. Its old sacred fig tree stands within a rampart, and the temple is held to have belonged with neighbouring shrines to a single monastic complex of the early Anuradhapura period.

name: Sri Pushparama Vihara, Ratmalana
significance: A Buddhist temple at Ratmalana in the Colombo District, built between 1795 and 1800 by Balapitiye Dheerananda Thera. The Sri Lankan government declared it a protected archaeological monument on 23 February 2007.

name: Delgamuwa Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (Sacred Tooth Relic, formerly hidden here)
significance: A Buddhist temple at Kuruwita in the Ratnapura District, remembered as the refuge of the Buddha's Tooth Relic during Portuguese rule: King Mayadunne of Sitawaka had the relic brought here about 1549, and it lay concealed inside a kurakkan grinding stone on the premises until Wimaladharmasuriya I recovered it in 1592 and carried it to Kandy.

name: Sri Pushparama Vihara, Balapitiya
style: preaching hall in colonial church manner
significance: A Buddhist temple at Balapitiya in the Galle District, headquarters of the Mulaghandi sect of the Amarapura Nikaya and a protected archaeological monument since 6 June 2008. The doors and windows of its dhamma preaching hall follow colonial church design, with two wooden stairs rising to a balcony that runs round the inner hall.

name: Asgiriya Raja Maha Vihara, Gampaha
deity: Gautama Buddha (Samadhi image; stone Buddha footprint)
significance: A cave temple at Gampaha in the Western Province whose foundation is traced to the reign of King Valagamba (89–77 BCE), with a 5th-century inscription found on its grounds. It keeps a Samadhi Buddha statue and flanking abhaya-mudra images carved in Kandyan-period manner, together with a stone bearing a footprint of the Buddha; the provincial ruler Sakalakala Wallabha patronised it under Parakramabahu VI.
story: The place is said to have taken the name Asgiri from a horse lost there by Prince Uttiya, brother of King Kelani Tissa.

name: Yatawatte Purana Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (stupa and tempita image house)
originNote: history traced to the reign of Parakramabahu VI (15th c.)
style: Tempita vihara (image house on granite pillars)
significance: A Buddhist temple about a kilometre from Gampaha town whose history is believed to reach back to the reign of Parakramabahu VI. Its tempita image house — of the type raised on granite pillars that was popular in Sri Lanka between the 17th and 19th centuries — is dated to 21 March 1861, and a stupa stands beside it.

name: Gonagolla Vihara
builtDisplay: 3rd c. BCE stupa; frescoes 3rd c. CE
significance: An ancient Buddhist site at Gonagolla in the Ampara District where a stupa and two ponds are dated to the third century BCE, surrounded by drip-ledged caves, a vatadage, stone stairways and carved pillars. Its third-century CE frescoes have earned it the local name Punchi Seegiriya, 'little Sigiriya', and rock inscriptions of the 3rd to 5th centuries record gifts by monks and by the wives of district governors.

name: Koskandawala Raja Maha Vihara
significance: An old Buddhist cave temple at Koskandawala in the Gampaha District, with a stupa and an image house. It is counted among neighbouring cave temples said to have formed a single monastic complex in the early Anuradhapura period.

name: Nagadeepa Purana Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (gem-studded throne; stone Buddha footprint)
builtDisplay: rebuilt under Devanampiya Tissa and Dutugemunu
significance: A Buddhist temple on the island of Nainativu off the Jaffna coast, revered as the place the Buddha visited to reconcile two Naga kings. It was rebuilt under Devanampiya Tissa and again under Dutugemunu, and keeps a stone bearing the Buddha's footprint along with a gem-studded throne given by Ratnapura businessmen in 2011.
story: The Buddha is said to have come here five years after his enlightenment to settle the quarrel of the Naga kings Chulodara and Mahodara over a gem-studded throne, converting them by his miracles.

name: Sri Dharmendrarama Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (Sri Pathul Gala footprint slabs)
significance: An archaeological Buddhist temple at Mayadunna in Gonagolla village, Ampara District, protected as an archaeological site since 10 October 2014. Its remains include a stupa, Buddha-footprint slabs, fragments of moonstones, building bases, pillars and a rock inscription — footprint slabs being among the objects used to represent the Buddha before statues of him were made.

name: Muwangala Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (Sri Pathul Gala footprint slabs)
significance: An archaeological Buddhist temple at Muwangala near Hingurana in the Ampara District, protected as an archaeological site since 26 December 2014. A third-century inscription there records a grant to the temple by a viceroy named Kodini, and the remains include a stupa, a drip-ledged cave, an asanaghara, Buddha-footprint slabs, moonstone fragments, building bases and pillars.

name: Asgiri Maha Viharaya
deity: Gautama Buddha (custodianship of the Sacred Tooth Relic)
significance: The Kandy monastery that heads the Asgiriya chapter of the Siyam Nikaya, one of the two chapters holding custody of the Buddha's Tooth Relic enshrined in the Sri Dalada Maligawa. Commander Siriwardhana founded it on the instructions of Parakramabahu IV of Kurunegala, and it was completed in 1302.
story: By another account the name Asgiri recalls Queen Chandrawathie, mother of King Vikramabahu, who was cremated in the burning ground of Adahana Maluva.

name: Nikasala Aranya Senasanaya
significance: An ancient Buddhist forest hermitage of cave-temple type at Kanduboda-Moragane village near Panduwasnuwara, in the Kurunegala District of Sri Lanka's North Western Province.

name: Aramanapola Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (image house; sacred Bodhi tree)
originNote: site traced to King Devanampiya Tissa (250–210 BCE)
significance: A Buddhist temple at Ganegama near Pelmadulla in the Ratnapura District whose history is traced to King Devanampiya Tissa and which Parakramabahu VI completed as a full temple in honour of his mother Sunethradevi; its name is said to recall monks brought from the Arammana country of Myanmar under Vijayabahu I to restore the order after Chola rule. Its Bodhi tree is held to be one of the thirty-two saplings of the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, and the largest of them.

name: Sri Saddharmagupta Piriven Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (image house and Bodhi tree)
significance: An old piriven vihara — a monastic teaching temple — at Dombawela in Udugampola, Gampaha District, recognised by the government as a protected archaeological monument. Its precinct holds a stupa, image house, Bodhi tree, bell tower, preaching hall, library and monks' dwellings, the old library building having been conserved in 2010.

name: Ibbagala Raja Maha Vihara
significance: An ancient Buddhist cave temple in the mid-valley of the Ethagala rock at Kurunegala, in Sri Lanka's North Western Province. Its title Raja Maha Vihara marks it as one of the temples that historically held royal patronage.

name: Yatala Vehera
deity: Buddha (relic caskets recovered from the stupa)
significance: A stupa at Deberawewa near Tissamaharama in the Hambantota District, dated to roughly the third century BCE and credited either to Yatala Tissa of Ruhuna or to his father Mahanaga. A large number of relic caskets has been recovered from it, and the restoration begun in 1883 took over a century to finish.
story: The stupa is said to have been raised over the place where the prince was born, and by another account to have been offered to Arittha, the first Sinhalese arahant.

name: Pilikuththuwa Raja Maha Vihara
builtDisplay: caves in use by the 2nd–3rd c. BCE
significance: A Buddhist cave temple at Pilikuththuwa in the Gampaha District, on ground inhabited since prehistoric times, whose caves appear to have served monks by the 2nd–3rd century BCE. The complex includes an image house and a dagoba.
story: King Valagamba is said to have sheltered here from time to time during the invasion from South India.

name: Degaldoruwa Raja Maha Vihara
significance: A rock-cut cave temple near Kandy, begun in 1771 during the reign of Kirti Sri Rajasinha and completed by his younger brother Rajadhi Rajasinha after he came to the throne. Behind two roofed ante-chambers the shrine cut into the rock holds a large reclining Buddha, and its walls carry celebrated murals of the Jataka stories and the Buddha's former births.
story: A farmer is said to have found golden sickles in a cleft between the boulders and to have borrowed one each day for his harvest until he tried to keep it, whereupon the guardian sealed the gap — and the king ordered a temple raised on the spot.

name: Magul Maha Viharaya
deity: Gautama Buddha (image shrine, stupa and Bodhi tree)
significance: A Buddhist temple at Lahugala in the Ampara District whose image shrine, stupa and sacred fig all survive in good condition. Tradition assigns its completion to King Kavantissa in the second century BCE, though other accounts credit King Dhatusena of the fifth century CE.
story: Magul means 'wedding' in Sinhala: the site is said to mark where Kavantissa married Viharamahadevi after the sea carried her miraculously ashore, and the foundations of the Magul Maduwa wedding pavilion are still shown there.

name: Samudrasanna Vihara
significance: A Buddhist temple at Mount Lavinia on the coast south of Colombo, completed in 1845. The Sri Lankan government declared it an archaeological protected site on 6 June 2008.

name: Mulkirigala Raja Maha Vihara
builtDisplay: 3rd c. BCE per the Mahavamsa; enlarged 5th and 18th c.
style: cave temple on a 205 m rock
significance: A cave temple cut into a 205-metre rock inland of Tangalle in the Hambantota District, credited by the Mahavamsa to King Saddhatissa and later enlarged under Dhatusena (461–479) and Kirti Sri Rajasinha (1747–1782). Its terraces of caves hold many Buddha images, among them the great reclining Buddha of the Paduma Rahath Vihara, and a Bodhi tree held to be one of the thirty-two saplings of the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi.
story: The rock is linked to the Jataka in which the Buddha, in an earlier birth, gave flesh from his own body to ransom a dove.

name: Lahugala Kiri Vehera
significance: An ancient Buddhist temple with a stupa at Lahugala in the Ampara District, believed to belong to the reign of King Dappula I in the seventh century.

name: Udayagiri Raja Maha Vihara
significance: A Buddhist temple at Udayagiri village in the Ampara District, protected as an archaeological monument since 26 December 2014. A stone pillar inscription records that two generals of King Udaya I exempted the vihara from taxes, and the site is said to go back more than a thousand years.

name: Kande Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (48.8 m seated image in bhumisparsha mudra)
significance: A hilltop Buddhist temple at Aluthgama in the Kalutara District, founded in 1734 by Karapagala Dewamitta Thera. Its precinct holds a stupa built in 1935, a relic chamber, an image house with Kandyan-era frescoes and a Bodhi tree reckoned over three hundred years old, and a seated Buddha 48.8 m high in bhumisparsha mudra, finished in 2007, now dominates the site.

name: Lahugala Kota Vehera
significance: A stupa at Lahugala in the Ampara District, one of only four structures of the Kota Vehera type known in Sri Lanka. Inscriptions at the site, of the first and second centuries CE, name kings including Bhatika Tissa, Kutakanna Tissa and Gajabahu I.

name: Galmaduwa Raja Maha Vihara, Ampara
builtDisplay: trad. King Saddha Tissa, 2nd c. BCE
significance: A Buddhist temple complex with a stupa at Galmaduwa near Hingurana in the Ampara District, believed to have been built during the reign of King Saddha Tissa of Anuradhapura in the second century BCE.

name: Pusulpitiya Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (Dambaran stone image; ancient Bo tree)
significance: A Buddhist temple at Pusulpitiya in the Nuwara Eliya District whose history is traced to the third century BCE or before. It keeps a Bo tree planted in the time of Devanampiya Tissa and one of the four Dambaran Buddha statues said to have been brought from India by Arahat Maliyadeva, and it sheltered the Sacred Tooth Relic on three occasions of political unrest.
story: An Indian brahmin hunting a golden ash pumpkin in the Kotmale country is said to have sacrificed his son to win it, then set it down on a rocky plain where it sank into the stone — giving Pusulpitiya its name.

name: Kshetrarama Maha Vihara
significance: A Buddhist temple at Moratuwa in the Colombo District, established in 1829 by the chief monk Ven. Weligama Sri Sumanatissa Thera. Its old image house holds a seated stone Buddha and the temple keeps ola-leaf volumes of the Tipitaka, while its Seema Malakaya shows architectural features found at no other Buddhist shrine in the country.
